title: Why Liquids Are Rare
question: What makes a liquid behave the way it does, and why is it so hard to find?
hook: Water covers our planet, yet liquids are the rarest state of matter in the known universe.
idea: Particles held by bonds of middling strength give liquids a fixed volume, a flexible shape and almost no squeeze.

beats.prompt: A valve in a water pipe is slammed shut. What happens inside the pipe?

choices.label: The water squeezes into a smaller space and absorbs the stop quietly
choices.feedback: Tempting, but liquids barely compress, so the water has nowhere to go.

choices.label: A big pressure spike forms at the valve and rushes backward through the system
The water simply stops moving, with no effect on the pipe
choices.feedback: Tempting, but the stopped flow has to go somewhere, and the pressure change travels through the liquid.

beats.explain: Liquids are nearly incompressible, so a sudden stop makes a huge pressure spike at the valve that travels backward at just under the speed of sound, banging the pipes.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of cavitation in order
items: Liquid in a low-pressure area vaporizes into bubbles
The bubbles enter high-pressure areas and collapse
Liquid rushes into the empty cavities with great local force
beats.explain: Bubbles form in low pressure and collapse in high pressure, and the liquid rushing in erodes whatever solid is next to it.

beats.prompt: Match each everyday mixture to the kind of liquid mixture it is
beats.explain: Everyday liquid mixtures come in several kinds, from solutions to emulsions, suspensions and colloids.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: So pressure at one point is passed on to every other part of the liquid.
So very little energy is lost to squeezing the liquid.
So a liquid can never be pulled apart, even in violent turbulence.
beats.explain: Because liquids have little elasticity, they can be pulled apart where there is high turbulence or a sharp change in direction.
